text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Centre Party leader Olof Johansson made no comment on media reports of a possible coalition between his party and the ruling Social Democrats. "I have the feeling that talk of such a coalition...has been initiated by people not directly involved," he said. Johansson said the party's congress next year would formulate its strategy for the next general election in 1998.

- Sweden's two largest investors in shares, AB Investor and the state's fourth AP pension fund, welcomed comments by Finance Minister Erik Asbrink that three other funds together worth 580 billion crowns might be allowed to buy shares rather than interest-bearing paper. "The spectre of fund socialism belongs to a forgotten era. It is time for all political parties to realise that," Investor's chief executive Claes Dahlback said.

- Opposition parties want more information from the government before a parliamentary decision in December whether to order more JAS 39 Gripen planes from the Saab-led consortium. The defence procurement agency FMV has discussed various options with the manufacturers, ranging from 40 to 64 additional planes.

- The possible relaxation of investment rules for state-controlled pension funds could be because the purchasing power of the funds for government bonds is no longer required, according to an analysis in the newspaper. The debate about use of money locked in the funds - a hot political potato in the 1980s - could now revolve on the issue of protecting Swedish ownership of share capital.

- Goran Johnsson, chairman of the metalworkers' union and a management board member of the ruling Social Democrats, said a possible coalition with the Centre Party was unlikely to bring the stability sought by Prime Minister Goran Persson. But the Centre's opposition to EMU membership and its energy policies would not promote economic growth, he believed.

- Swedes are uncertain about their economic future and are therefore consuming less, which in turn dampens prospects for expansion and the creation of new jobs, according to the analysts of TCO, the civil servants' union.

- Finance Minister Asbrink's talk of loosening the reins on the first three state pension funds was a factor behind yesterday's 1.7 percent bourse index rise. "When foreign ownership (of shares) is on the increase, it is appropriate to do something about Swedish ownership," Asbrink said earlier.

- Insurer Skandia is following its competitors and lowering prices in the life market. From November 18 Skandia will introduce a new price structure, after Trygg Hansa took the initiative last spring with a hefty reduction in charges.

- The bourse is about to obtain its second listed mountain resort company - Investment AB Bure, which is buying the company operating lifts in leading ski resort Are. OTC-listed Lindvallen has shown a steady profit even in the depth of the early 1990s recession.
